statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a first apotome, the âsideâ of the area is an apotome.
heath_proof: For let the area AB be contained by the rational straight line AC and the first apotome AD; I say that the “side” of the area AB is an apotome. For, since AD is a first apotome, let DG be its annex; therefore AG, GD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. [X. 73] And the whole AG is commensurable with the rational straight line AC set out, and the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AG; [X. Deff. III. 1] if therefore there be applied to AG a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on DG and deficient by a square figure, it divides it into commensurable parts. [X. 17] Let DG be bisected at E, let there be applied to AG a parallelogram equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure, and let it be the rectangle AF, FG; therefore AF is commensurable with FG. And through the points E, F, G let EH, FI, GK be drawn parallel to AC. Now, since AF is commensurable in length with FG, therefore AG is also commensurable in length with each of the straight lines AF, FG. [X. 15] But AG is commensurable with AC; therefore each of the straight lines AF, FG is commensurable in length with AC. [X. 12] And AC is rational; therefore each of the straight lines AF, FG is also rational, so that each of the rectangles AI, FK is also rational. [X. 19] Now, since DE is commensurable in length with EG, therefore DG is also commensurable in length with each of the straight lines DE, EG. [X. 15] But DG is rational and incommensurable in length with AC; therefore each of the straight lines DE, EG is also rational and incommensurable in length with AC; [X. 13] therefore each of the rectangles DH, EK is medial. [X. 21] Now let the square LM be made equal to AI, and let there be subtracted the square NO having a common angle with it, the angle LPM, and equal to FK; therefore the squares LM, NO are about the same diameter. [VI. 26] Let PR be their diameter, and let the figure be drawn. Since then the rectangle contained by AF, FG is equal to the square on EG, therefore, as AF is to EG, so is EG to FG. [VI. 17] But, as AF is to EG, so is AI to EK, and, as EG is to FG, so is EK to KF; [VI. 1] therefore EK is a mean proportional between AI, KF. [V. 11] But MN is also a mean proportional between LM, NO, as was before proved, [Lemma after X. 53] and AI is equal to the square LM, and KF to NO; therefore MN is also equal to EK. But EK is equal to DH, and MN to LO; therefore DK is equal to the gnomon UVW and NO. But AK is also equal to the squares LM, NO; therefore the remainder AB is equal to ST. But ST is the square on LN; therefore the square on LN is equal to AB; therefore LN is the “side” of AB. I say next that LN is an apotome. For, since each of the rectangles AI, FK is rational, and they are equal to LM, NO, therefore each of the squares LM, NO, that is, the squares on LP, PN respectively, is also rational; therefore each of the straight lines LP, PN is also rational. Again, since DH is medial and is equal to LO, therefore LO is also medial. Since then LO is medial, while NO is rational, therefore LO is incommensurable with NO. But, as LO is to NO, so is LP to PN; [VI. 1] therefore LP is incommensurable in length with PN. [X. 11] And both are rational; therefore LP, PN are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore LN is an apotome. [X. 73] And it is the “side” of the area AB; therefore the “side” of the area AB is an apotome.

10.91
**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a first apotome, the âsideâ of the area is an apotome.

**Step 1.** Let the area be contained by the rational straight line AC and the first apotome AD. I say that the "side" of the area AC * AD is an apotome.

**Step 2.** Since AD is a first apotome, let DG be the annex to AD, so that AG and GD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AG, and AG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC set out [D10.3.1].

**Step 3.** Bisect DG at the point E [1.10], and to AG apply a parallelogram equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure; let this be the rectangle AF by FG [6.28]. Then, since the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AG, and to the whole AG there has been applied the rectangle AF by FG equal to the fourth part of the square on DG (since EG is half of DG) and deficient by a square figure, therefore AF is commensurable in length with FG [10.17].

**Step 4.** Since AG is commensurable in length with AC, the whole AG is rational and commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC. Therefore the rectangle AC by AG is rational [10.19]. But AG equals AF + FG, and AF is commensurable in length with FG [Step 3].

**Step 5.** Now since AF is commensurable in length with FG, and AG is commensurable in length with each of AF and FG [10.15], and AG is commensurable in length with AC, therefore each of AF and FG is also commensurable in length with AC [10.12]. Hence each of AF and FG is rational and commensurable in length with AC.

**Step 6.** Therefore the rectangles AC by AF and AC by FG are each rational [10.19].

**Step 7.** Now, since DG is bisected at E, and the rectangle AF by FG equals the square on EG [Step 3 construction], we have by [2.5] that the rectangle AF by FG together with the square on AG minus the mean (i.e., the square on EG) relates to the segments. More precisely, since AF * FG = EG^2 and DG = 2*EG, we have AF * FG = (DG/2)^2 = DG^2/4.

**Step 8.** Let the square on H be made equal to the rectangle AC by AF, and the square on K be made equal to the rectangle AC by FG. Then the squares on H and K together equal AC * AF + AC * FG = AC * AG (since AF + FG = AG). That is, the squares on H and K together equal the rectangle AC by AG, which is rational [Step 5, 10.19]. So the sum of the squares on H and K is rational.

**Step 9.** Since AC * AF = H^2 and AC * FG = K^2, and these are both rational areas [Step 6], H and K are each rational straight lines [D10.1.4].

**Step 10.** Now consider the rectangle H by K. We have (H * K)^2 = H^2 * K^2 = (AC * AF)(AC * FG) = AC^2 * AF * FG. Also, AF * FG = EG^2 = DG^2/4 [Step 7]. Therefore (H * K)^2 = AC^2 * DG^2/4 = (AC * DG/2)^2, so H * K = AC * DG/2, meaning 2 * H * K = AC * DG.

**Step 11.** Now the rectangle AC by DG: since GD is the annex to the first apotome, GD is rational but incommensurable in length with AC (for if GD were commensurable in length with AC, then since AG is also commensurable in length with AC, AG and GD would be commensurable in length with each other [10.12], contradicting that they are commensurable in square only). Therefore AC and GD are rational and commensurable in square only, so the rectangle AC by GD is medial [10.21].

**Step 12.** Since 2 * H * K = AC * DG [Step 10], twice the rectangle contained by H and K is medial. Therefore the rectangle H by K is medial [Step 11]. But the sum of the squares on H and K is rational [Step 8].

**Step 13.** Now I must show that H and K are incommensurable in square. Since AC * AF = H^2 and AC * FG = K^2, we have H^2 : K^2 = AF : FG [6.1]. Since AF and FG are commensurable in length [Step 3], AF : FG is a ratio of number to number [10.5], so H^2 : K^2 is a ratio of number to number, meaning H and K are commensurable in square [10.9]. But then H and K are rational and commensurable in square. We must determine whether they are commensurable in length or in square only.

**Step 14.** Since H^2 : K^2 = AF : FG, and AF is commensurable in length with FG, H is commensurable in square with K. Now AF and FG are commensurable in length, so AF : FG is rational. But H^2 = AC * AF and K^2 = AC * FG, so H^2 : K^2 = AF : FG. For H and K to be commensurable in length, we would need H : K to be a ratio of number to number, i.e., AF : FG to be a ratio of a square number to a square number [10.9]. But there is no reason this must hold in general; AF and FG being commensurable in length means their ratio is of number to number, but not necessarily of square to square.

**Step 15.** Let me reconsider the construction more carefully. The area to be "sided" is AC * AD, where AD = AG - GD (the apotome). So the area equals AC * AG - AC * GD. We have AC * AG = H^2 + K^2 [Step 8] and AC * GD = 2*H*K [Step 10]. Therefore AC * AD = H^2 + K^2 - 2*H*K = (H - K)^2 [2.7, since H > K as AF > FG]. Thus the "side" of the area AC * AD is H - K.

**Step 16.** Now H and K are rational straight lines [Step 9]. We need to show H - K is an apotome, i.e., that H and K are commensurable in square only [10.73].

**Step 17.** Suppose for contradiction that H and K are commensurable in length. Then H^2 + K^2 and H * K are commensurable [by 10.15 applied to the commensurability of H^2 with K^2 when H is commensurable in length with K]. But H^2 + K^2 is rational [Step 8] and H * K is medial [Step 12], which means a rational area would be commensurable with a medial area, contradicting the fact that rational and medial areas are incommensurable [10.26, since a rational area cannot be commensurable with a medial area -- indeed, if H^2 + K^2 were commensurable with H*K, then since H^2 + K^2 is rational, H*K would also be rational by 10.12 applied to areas, contradicting that H*K is medial].

**Step 18.** More precisely: if H and K are commensurable in length, then H^2 is commensurable with H*K (since H^2 : H*K = H : K, a ratio of number to number, hence commensurable by 10.6). Similarly K^2 is commensurable with H*K. Therefore H^2 + K^2 is commensurable with H*K [10.15, 10.12]. But H^2 + K^2 is rational and 2*H*K is medial. Since H^2 + K^2 is commensurable with H*K, and 2*H*K is commensurable with H*K (differing by a factor of 2), H^2 + K^2 would be commensurable with 2*H*K. A rational area commensurable with a medial area is impossible, for a medial area is by definition irrational [D10.1.4, 10.21], while a rational area is rational. Two areas that are commensurable are either both rational or both irrational [by the nature of commensurability with the assigned rational square]. This is a contradiction.

**Step 19.** Therefore H and K are not commensurable in length. Since H and K are rational straight lines (commensurable in square with the assigned rational line), and they are not commensurable in length, they are commensurable in square only.

**Step 20.** Since H and K are rational and commensurable in square only, H - K is an apotome [10.73].

**Step 21.** And (H - K)^2 = AC * AD [Step 15], so the "side" of the area contained by the rational straight line AC and the first apotome AD is H - K, which is an apotome. Q.E.D.
